title: Social Cognition Assessment
shortDescription: Reading intentions, perspective-taking, and interpreting social scenarios — the cognitive side of understanding people.
longDescription: Social Cognition is built around the paradigm of Happé's Strange Stories Task (Happé, 1994), the most widely cited theory-of-mind test beyond childhood — short vignettes end in a character saying something that isn't literally true (a lie, a joke, sarcasm, a white lie, pretense), and understanding why requires reasoning about what the character believes, wants, or intends. The original task is administered verbally with open-ended responses hand-coded by a researcher; here every vignette is answered as a forced choice between the correct mental-state explanation and plausible-but-wrong alternatives, so it can be scored deterministically.
sourceNote: Original vignettes written to implement Happé's Strange Stories Task paradigm (non-literal-language types documented in Happé 1994 and White, Hill, Happé & Frith 2009: lie, white lie, joke, pretense, misunderstanding, persuasion, appearance/reality, figure of speech, irony) — the original published stories are not reproduced. Known adaptation: the real task scores open verbal explanations on a 0/1/2 mental-state scale via trained coders; this version uses forced-choice answers (the correct mentalistic explanation vs. a literal/physical-state distractor and an unrelated distractor) so it can be scored deterministically without human coding — this measures the same core skill (attributing the right mental state) but is an easier recognition task than free explanation.

sections.name: Non-Literal Language
sections.description: Understanding lies, white lies, jokes, irony, and figures of speech — statements that aren't literally true but make sense once you understand why they were said.
sections.instructions: Read each short scenario, then choose the explanation that best captures why the character said what they said.

sections.name: Social Reasoning
sections.description: Understanding misunderstandings, persuasion, and pretense — situations that require tracking what someone else believes or intends, separate from what's actually true.
sections.instructions: Read each short scenario, then choose the explanation that best accounts for the character's behavior.

scoringDimensions.label: Social Cognition
scoringDimensions.description: Composite score across non-literal language and social reasoning.

scoringDimensions.label: Non-Literal Language
scoringDimensions.description: Correctly interpreting lies, jokes, irony, and figurative speech.

scoringDimensions.label: Social Reasoning
scoringDimensions.description: Tracking beliefs, intentions, and misunderstandings distinct from objective reality.

resultRanges.title: Developing
resultRanges.description: Social scenarios are often read at face value — the literal words rather than what the speaker actually believed, wanted, or intended.
recommendations: When someone says something surprising, pause and ask what they might believe that would make it make sense
Practice noticing the difference between what's said and what's meant in conversations you observe
Watch for social cues like tone and context that signal irony, jokes, or tact

resultRanges.title: Average
resultRanges.description: Straightforward social cues like obvious jokes or lies are read correctly, but subtler cases — white lies, persuasion, double meanings — are harder to untangle.
recommendations: Practice distinguishing white lies (said to protect feelings) from ordinary lies (said for self-interest)
Pay attention to a speaker's likely goal, not just their literal words, when interpreting persuasion

resultRanges.title: Strong
resultRanges.description: Reliably infers what other people believe and intend, correctly separating that from objective reality in most scenarios.
recommendations: Practice with layered scenarios where a character's belief is itself mistaken
Apply this skill deliberately in real conversations — check your read against what actually happened

resultRanges.title: Very Strong
resultRanges.description: Consistently accurate at reading intentions, irony, and non-literal language, rarely taking a figurative statement at face value.
recommendations: This is a strong foundation for roles involving negotiation, mediation, or coaching
Notice how this skill helps you catch misunderstandings before they escalate

resultRanges.title: Exceptional
resultRanges.description: Expert-level social cognition — mental states, intentions, and non-literal meaning are read quickly and accurately across every scenario type.
recommendations: Consider where this strength is most valuable — teaching, therapy, leadership, and mediation all lean on it heavily
Mentor others on distinguishing what's said from what's meant

questions.questionText: Tom ate the last slice of cake that was meant for his sister's birthday. When his mom asked who ate it, Tom said, "I don't know, maybe the dog got it." Why did Tom say that?

options.label: Tom wanted his mom to believe something false so he wouldn't get in trouble
Tom genuinely thought the dog might have eaten it
Tom likes dogs

questions.questionText: Grandma knitted Lily a sweater with a wonky sleeve. Lily doesn't like it, but she says, "Thank you Grandma, I love it!" Why did Lily say that?

options.label: Lily actually loves the sweater and just seemed unhappy
Lily wanted to protect Grandma's feelings rather than say something hurtful
Lily is planning to return the sweater to the store

questions.questionText: Dan says to his friend, "Nice haircut — did you lose a bet?" His friend laughs. Why did Dan say that?

options.label: Dan is teasing his friend playfully, not seriously criticizing the haircut
Dan genuinely believes his friend lost a bet
Dan doesn't know what a haircut is

questions.questionText: It's pouring rain and the picnic is ruined. Mia looks up at the sky and says, "Oh great, perfect weather for a picnic." What does Mia mean?

options.label: Mia thinks it's actually good weather for a picnic
Mia means the opposite — she's frustrated that the weather ruined the picnic
Mia is asking a genuine question about the forecast

questions.questionText: After a long, exhausting hike, Ravi collapses on the couch and says, "I could sleep for a year." What does Ravi mean?

options.label: Ravi is extremely tired and wants to convey how tired he is, not that he'll literally sleep for a year
Ravi has a sleep disorder
Ravi is planning to hibernate

questions.questionText: Jake borrowed his roommate's charger and lost it. When asked where it is, Jake says, "I gave it back to you already." This isn't true — why did Jake say it?

options.label: Jake is confused about which charger is being discussed
Jake wants his roommate to falsely believe the charger was returned, so he avoids blame
Jake is joking around

questions.questionText: A coworker asks Priya, "How do I look for the interview?" His shirt is inside out but there's no time to fix it. Priya says, "You look great — good luck!" Why might Priya say that instead of pointing out the shirt?

options.label: Priya didn't notice the shirt was inside out
With no time left to fix it, pointing it out would only add stress without helping — so Priya chose encouragement instead
Priya genuinely thinks an inside-out shirt looks great

questions.questionText: Sam trips and drops his lunch tray in the crowded cafeteria. His friend says, "Smooth move." What does the friend mean?

options.label: The friend is sincerely complimenting Sam's coordination
The friend is teasing Sam — the opposite of "smooth" just happened
The friend didn't see what happened

questions.questionText: At dinner, Dad says, "I'm not a doctor, but I'm pretty sure that's not how you're supposed to eat spaghetti," watching his toddler smear sauce everywhere. Everyone laughs. What's happening?

options.label: Dad is making a lighthearted joke about the mess, not giving real medical advice
Dad is a doctor and is being modest
Dad is genuinely worried about food safety

questions.questionText: After hearing the shocking news, Elena says, "You could've knocked me over with a feather." What does Elena mean?

options.label: Elena was extremely surprised — not that she was literally almost knocked over
Elena is physically weak
Elena wants someone to bring her a feather

questions.questionText: Ben texts "running late, sorry!" to the group chat for game night. He meant to send it to his other friends about a different plan — he'd actually already left for game night on time. When he arrives on time, his friends are confused. Why?

options.label: Ben's friends believed the text was about game night, so they expected him to be late — but it was actually about something else
Ben's friends don't know how to read texts
Ben actually was late and is lying about it

questions.questionText: A salesperson tells a customer, "This is the last one in stock, and three other people are asking about it." Why might the salesperson say this?

options.label: To create a sense of urgency that makes the customer more likely to buy now
To warn the customer that the product is unpopular
Because store policy requires mentioning stock levels

questions.questionText: Two kids are playing. One picks up a banana, holds it to her ear, and says, "Hello? Yes, one moment please." Then hands it to her friend. What is she doing?

options.label: Pretending the banana is a phone, as part of imaginative play
She genuinely believes the banana is a phone
She is hungry and confused

questions.questionText: Aisha waves enthusiastically across the street. The person doesn't wave back and walks away. Aisha feels hurt — but it turns out the person wasn't looking in her direction at all and never saw her. Why did Aisha feel hurt?

options.label: Aisha believed the person saw her and chose to ignore her, even though that wasn't actually true
Aisha doesn't like the person
The person deliberately ignored her

questions.questionText: A manager tells the team, "I know this deadline is tight, but I really believe in this team's ability to pull it off." Why might the manager phrase it this way rather than just saying "finish it by Friday"?

options.label: To motivate the team by expressing confidence, making them more willing to push through the tight deadline
The manager is unsure whether Friday is actually the deadline
Company policy requires compliments before every deadline

questions.questionText: A child sets up stuffed animals in a row and says, "Class, today we're learning about dinosaurs," pointing to a picture book. What is happening?

options.label: The child is play-acting being a teacher, treating the stuffed animals as students
The child believes the stuffed animals can actually learn
The child is doing actual homework

questions.questionText: Leo tells his friend a surprise party is "definitely not happening this weekend" so his friend won't suspect anything — but the party actually is this weekend. His friend repeats this to someone else as fact. Why did the friend get it wrong?

options.label: The friend believed what Leo said was true, not knowing Leo said it deliberately to protect the surprise
The friend also knows about the surprise and is playing along
There is no surprise party

questions.questionText: Before asking to borrow the car, a teenager first does the dishes without being asked and compliments dinner. Why might they be doing this?

options.label: Putting their parent in a good mood first, making them more likely to say yes to the car request
The teenager just enjoys doing dishes
It's their assigned chore day

questions.questionText: Two friends agree to meet "at the usual place" — but one means their usual coffee shop and the other means their usual park bench. Both wait separately, confused when the other doesn't show. Why?

options.label: Each believed "the usual place" meant the same thing to both of them, when it actually referred to two different places
One of them forgot about the plan entirely
They were never actually friends

questions.questionText: An ad says, "9 out of 10 dentists recommend this toothpaste" without mentioning how many dentists were actually asked or how they were chosen. Why might an advertiser phrase a claim this way?

options.label: To make the product sound more credible and trustworthy than the underlying evidence necessarily supports
Because exactly 10 dentists exist in total
It's a legal requirement for toothpaste ads
